name: When I Work
subcategory: HR, recruiting, payroll and workforce operations
tagline: Build a small shift schedule, availability form, and swap approval workflow

tiers.name: Essentials
tiers.limits: Scheduling and team messaging; price per user/month

tiers.name: Pro
tiers.limits: Expanded scheduling, controls, and reporting; price per user/month

tiers.name: Premium
tiers.limits: Advanced scheduling and workforce controls; price per user/month

pricing.freeTierCaps: no free tier; 14-day trial with no card
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual (annual is prepaid and 5% lower)
pricing.hiddenCosts: Time Tracking & Attendance is a separately toggled add-on with no public price on the live plan table. Annual plans cannot reduce seats or downgrade until within 30 days of renewal, use manual renewal, and are non-refundable.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For When I Work, build a small shift schedule, availability form, and swap approval workflow. The hard boundary is mobile apps, time clock, notifications, scheduling edge cases, and support, plus compliance, payroll, and regulated integrations.
coreLoopDIY: Build a small shift schedule, availability form, and swap approval workflow, maintain approvals and records, and export data without calculating payroll or making employment decisions.
whatYouLose: mobile apps, time clock, notifications, scheduling edge cases, and support
identity checks and global employment infrastructure
ongoingBurden: sensitive data, access, retention, audit, payroll calculations, filings, benefits, employment law, incident response, and support
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for When I Work because HR platforms survive because mistakes affect pay, benefits, immigration, and legal obligations, not because forms are difficult to render. The recurring cost buys sensitive data, access, retention, audit, payroll calculations, filings, benefits, employment law, incident response, and support, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Frappe HR
priorArt.desc: Active open-source human-resources and payroll application built on Frappe.

alternatives.name: Sling Free
alternatives.desc: Schedules, availability and manager-approved swaps for 30 people; the time clock costs extra.

facts.install: Hosted signup, then invite employees by email or phone to the web, iOS and Android apps
facts.dataFormat: Schedules, availability, requests and messages in Sling's cloud account; schedules and many records export as CSV or XLS
facts.gapVsPaid: It covers scheduling for thirty users but the free plan omits the time clock and several labor-management features.

alternatives.name: 7shifts Comp
alternatives.desc: A small roster, availability form and approved shift trades for one 15-person location.

facts.install: Hosted signup for one restaurant location, then invite staff to the web and mobile apps
facts.dataFormat: Employee profiles, schedules, availability, time-off and communications in 7shifts' cloud, with selected reports and export tools
facts.gapVsPaid: The free plan is restaurant-specific, limited to one location and fifteen employees, and lacks a free time clock.

alternatives.name: Connecteam Small Business Plan
alternatives.desc: Scheduling, availability and shift changes for ten people; employee eleven ends the free plan.

facts.install: Hosted signup, then invite staff to the web and mobile apps
facts.dataFormat: Employee records, documents, schedules and time data in Connecteam's cloud; schedules and timesheets export to Excel, PDF, CSV or payroll-specific files
facts.gapVsPaid: It is clean for ten users, but employee eleven ends the free plan and the product is broader than a dedicated scheduler.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Findmyshift Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Free forever for five staff, but one week of forward planning and no shift templates is too cramped for an ongoing roster.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Homebase Basic
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The free schedule is real, but availability, time-off requests and shift trades require a paid plan.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Jibble Scheduling
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The scheduling product still says Coming soon.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Essentials plan and a internal records tracker without payroll DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for When I Work in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: build a small shift schedule, availability form, and swap approval workflow, maintain approvals and records, and export data without calculating payroll or making employment decisions.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement employees, teams, roles, documents, leave requests, equipment, onboarding tasks, and acknowledgements.
Use least-privilege roles and log every read or change to sensitive records.
Add approval workflows, expiry reminders, export, retention, deletion holds, and encrypted backups.
Keep compensation fields optional and never calculate payroll, taxes, benefits, or statutory filings.
Provide a data dictionary and explain which fields should not be stored without legal review.
Ship Docker Compose, health checks, disaster recovery, and an emergency-access procedure.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out payroll calculation or money movement.
Deliberately leave out automated hiring decisions or applicant scoring.
Deliberately leave out tax, benefits, immigration, identity, and global-employment compliance.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
